section.title: Zion's New Name
section.sectionRationale: This chapter answers the shame of a forsaken city with new names, Hephzibah, My Delight Is in Her, and Beulah, Married, and pictures God rejoicing over Zion the way a bridegroom rejoices over a bride. Watchmen are posted who will not rest until Jerusalem's praise fills the earth, and the chapter closes with a herald announcing her Savior comes.
section.thesis: God renames a city once called Forsaken and Desolate with names of delight and marriage, promising to rejoice over her as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, and commissions restless watchmen and a highway-building people to prepare the way until He is seen to come.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a new name that the LORD's own mouth will bestow; no longer Forsaken but Hephzibah and Beulah; and prepare the way, for your salvation comes.

units.label: A new name from the LORD's own mouth
units.note: for Zion's sake I will not keep silent

verses.text: For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still, until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch.
Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory. You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow.
You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God.

units.label: Hephzibah and Beulah
units.note: as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride

verses.text: No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called {{hephzibah|Hephzibah}}, and your land {{beulah|Beulah}}; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride.
For as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you; and as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have posted watchmen; they will never be silent day or night. You who call on the LORD shall take no rest for yourselves,
nor give Him any rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth.
The LORD has sworn by His right hand and by His mighty arm: “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food, nor will foreigners drink the new wine for which you have toiled.
For those who harvest grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather grapes will drink the wine in My holy courts.”

units.label: Prepare the way, your salvation comes
units.note: Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken

verses.text: Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people! Build it up, build up the highway; clear away the stones; raise a banner for the nations!
Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth, “Say to Daughter Zion: See, your Savior comes! Look, His reward is with Him, and His recompense goes before Him.”
And they will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.

hephzibah.gloss: My delight is in her, a new name replacing Forsaken. It reverses the shame of exile with an intensely personal declaration of God's own pleasure in His people, the same delight language later echoed at Jesus' baptism, this is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, Matthew 3:17.

beulah.gloss: Married, possessed as a wife. Replacing the name Desolate, it pictures the land itself as a bride joined to the LORD, an image of covenant intimacy restored, the same marital metaphor Paul later uses of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32.

basic.context: A city once called Forsaken and Desolate is given new names, Hephzibah, My Delight Is in Her, and Beulah, Married, pictures of intimate covenant restoration. God commissions watchmen who will not rest until Jerusalem becomes the praise of the earth, and the chapter closes announcing that Zion's Savior comes.
basic.hermeneutics: The renaming is not cosmetic, it describes an actual change in relationship and status, from shame to delight, from desolation to marriage. The watchmen who give God no rest model a kind of prayer that actively partners with God's own stated resolve, verse 1, I will not keep silent.
basic.originalLanguages: The new names, hephtzi-bah, my delight is in her, and be'ulah, married, reverse the shame of Forsaken and Desolate with the language of personal delight and marital intimacy, the same register of delight God uses of His own Son at His baptism.
basic.typology: The bridegroom who rejoices over his bride anticipates Christ's relationship to the church, His bride, and the herald announcing behold, your Savior comes anticipates both the incarnation and Christ's triumphal entry, where crowds prepared His way with garments spread on the road.
basic.christ: The bridegroom imagery of verse 5 finds its full sense in Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:25-27, where Paul describes Christ loving the church as a bridegroom loves a bride, sanctifying her to present her to Himself in splendor. And Matthew 21:5 draws on this chapter's herald language, behold, your king is coming to you, quoted of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
basic.god: God refuses to keep silent about His people's shame, actively working and speaking until it is reversed; He is not a distant deity satisfied with mere improvement but a bridegroom who delights personally and specifically in the one He has redeemed.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5:25-27 describes Christ as bridegroom sanctifying the church, His bride. Matthew 21:5 echoes this chapter's herald announcing the coming king. Revelation 21:2 pictures the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
basic.oneStory: A city renamed from Forsaken to My Delight Is in Her, from Desolate to Married, tells the whole Bible's story in miniature, God does not merely rescue His people from shame, He draws them into the closest possible relationship, the intimacy of marriage, fulfilled and consummated when Christ presents His bride, the church, to Himself in splendor.

context.literary:
Isaiah 62 is built around names. The chapter promises a new name in verse 2, spells out two of them in verse 4, and closes with four more in verse 12. Between those poles come two scenes of action, the watchmen on the walls in verses 6 and 7 and the oath about grain and wine in verses 8 and 9. The shape is a frame of naming around a centre of persistent prayer and secure provision.

The names in verse 4 are given as a before and after. 'Forsaken' and 'Desolate' are replaced by 'Hephzibah' and 'Beulah', and the footnotes of the BSB give the older names in Hebrew as Azubah and Shemamah. Verse 12 repeats the movement: the people are called the Holy People and the Redeemed of the LORD, and the city is called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken. The word 'forsaken' in verse 4 and again in verse 12 binds the two ends together. What the chapter opens by cancelling, it closes by confirming.

Another thread is silence and speech. In verse 1 the speaker says 'I will not keep silent' and 'I will not keep still'. In verse 6 the watchmen 'will never be silent day or night', and verse 7 tells them to 'give Him no rest'. The verb for silence in verse 1 is the same one in verse 6, so the speaker's resolve is mirrored by the watchmen's. Then verse 11 shows what the speech finally delivers, a proclamation to the ends of the earth.

The chapter belongs with the two before it. In chapter 60 the city shines, in 61 the Anointed One brings good news, and in 62 the city is given a name and a bridegroom. The reader has seen the light, the herald and now the wedding. The 'I' of verse 1 shares the voice of 61:1 and there is no heading to mark a change of speaker.
context.historical:
To walk the walls of Jerusalem after the exile was to see how exposed the city was. Nehemiah describes gates burned, walls broken and the need to appoint guards at their posts and to keep the gates closed until the sun was hot, Nehemiah 2:17 and 7:3. Watchmen were therefore a real part of city life, and the first hearers would have pictured sentries on the ramparts looking for danger or for the first sign of a messenger. Isaiah had condemned the earlier watchmen of Israel as blind and 'mute dogs' that could not bark, Isaiah 56:10. Here the LORD Himself appoints watchmen who never stop speaking.

Verse 8 draws on the covenant curses. In Deuteronomy 28:33 the curse for covenant breaking was that a foreign people would eat the produce of the land and all the toil of the farmer, and the book of Judges records Midianite raiders who stripped the harvest, Judges 6:3-6. The exile and the years after had often meant that those who sowed did not eat. The LORD now swears by His right hand and mighty arm that this will not happen again. An oath sworn on God's own strength was the most solemn that could be made.

Verse 9 describes the opposite: those who harvest will eat, and those who gather grapes will drink in the LORD's holy courts. This looks back to the law that the tithe and festival offerings were to be eaten before the LORD with one's household, Deuteronomy 12:17-18. Harvest is joined to worship.

Names carried weight in Israel. Azubah and Hephzibah were ordinary names for women, borne by the mothers of kings, 1 Kings 22:42 and 2 Kings 21:1, and God had earlier renamed Abram and Jacob, Genesis 17:5 and 32:28. To give a city a new name was to declare a new identity, as when Jerusalem was to be called the City of Righteousness, Isaiah 1:26, or 'The LORD Is There', Ezekiel 48:35. The highway of verse 10 recalls the road for the returning exiles, Isaiah 40:3 and 57:14, and the banner for the nations recalls Isaiah 11:12.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 62 sits in a long line of passages about God and His people as husband and wife. Hosea has the LORD betroth Israel to Himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and compassion, Hosea 2:19-20. Jeremiah remembers 'your love as a bride' in the wilderness, Jeremiah 2:2. Isaiah 54:4-6 tells the forsaken wife that her Maker is her husband and that the LORD has called her back, and Zephaniah 3:17 pictures God rejoicing over His people with singing. Isaiah 62:4-5 carries the picture to its warmest point, and Isaiah 65:19 repeats that He will rejoice in Jerusalem and delight in His people.

The theme of the new name runs on beyond this chapter. Isaiah 65:15 says God's servants will be given another name. In Revelation 2:17 the one who overcomes is given a white stone with a new name, and in Revelation 3:12 Christ promises to write on the overcomer the name of God, the name of the city of God and His own new name. The renaming of Zion becomes the renaming of every believer.

Verse 11 borrows from Isaiah 40, where the herald is told to say 'Here is your God', and where the reward and recompense are with Him, Isaiah 40:9-10. It is quoted in Matthew 21:5, where the opening words 'Say to the Daughter of Zion' are joined to Zechariah 9:9 at the entry into Jerusalem. The Redeemed of the LORD in verse 12 recall the title of the Redeemer in Isaiah 59:20 and 60:16. The promise that the reward is with Him returns almost word for word in Revelation 22:12. The marriage of the Lamb in Revelation 19 and the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride in Revelation 21:2 give the chapter its New Testament completion.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet's first purpose was to answer the fear that God had finished with His people. 'The LORD has forsaken me,' Zion had said, Isaiah 49:14, and the returned community could easily feel the same, living in a small town of ruins. The chapter's reply is not to deny the history of abandonment but to say that it will be reversed by the one who named her. The names are God's own gift, bestowed by 'the mouth of the LORD', and so they are not open to being revised by circumstances.

He also wanted the hearers to take part in what God was doing. The watchmen on the walls are told never to be silent and to give God no rest until He establishes Jerusalem. Prayer here is not a way of changing God's mind but of aligning with His stated purpose, for verse 1 says He Himself will not keep silent. The hearers are meant to be a praying people who hold God to His promises.

A third aim is to bring the people from passivity to preparation. 'Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people!' The work of clearing stones and raising a banner is something the community is told to do, even though the promise is that the Savior is coming. The hope is not an excuse for sitting still.

Finally he wanted them to understand the kind of love God has for them. The marriage language of verse 5 is plain, and it says that God's delight in His people is personal and joyful. The first hearers were meant to hear that the God who judged them is also the God who rejoices over them, and that the names they carried in shame would be replaced by names of delight.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter contains a few commands, to the watchmen to keep praying and to the people to go out, build the highway, clear stones and raise a banner. These are addressed to a particular community at a particular time, yet the principle carries over: those who hold promises of God are to pray persistently and to prepare for what He will do. Jesus teaches persistent prayer in the parable of the widow, in which He asks whether God will not bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night, Luke 18:1-8.

Much of the chapter describes what God will do and how He regards His people. The marriage language is an image of God's love and does not give a pattern for any particular human marriage. The talk of kings seeing the city's glory, of the nations looking on and of foreigners no longer drinking the new wine describes the reversal of Israel's situation, and the church should not read it as promising political advantage.

The proper application is to read the new names as promises that belong to those in Christ. Peter says that those who were not a people are now the people of God and have received mercy, 1 Peter 2:10. The believer does not claim the chapter's earthly details for himself. He takes from it the certainty that God delights in His people, that He has appointed a watch of prayer, and that the Savior who comes is bringing His reward.

debates.question: Who are the watchmen of verses 6 and 7?

views.label: Prophets and spiritual leaders
views.case: Watchmen are an old image for prophets, as in Ezekiel 33:7, where the prophet is made a watchman for Israel. Isaiah 56:10 has condemned the blind watchmen of the earlier leadership, so the LORD now sets true ones in their place. On this reading the watchmen are the faithful prophetic voices who keep calling on God for the city.

views.label: Angels or heavenly beings
views.case: The verse says 'I have posted watchmen', as though they were appointed from outside the city. Some ancient interpreters took these to be angelic guardians who keep the matter of Jerusalem before God. The text does not say so, and the instruction in verse 6, 'You who call on the LORD', is addressed to people.

views.label: All of God's people who pray
views.case: The command to give God no rest is addressed to anyone who calls on the LORD. In the New Testament believers are urged to pray at all times and not lose heart, Luke 18:1, and to watch, Mark 13:37. Many readers apply the image to the whole praying community, with leaders carrying a special share, Hebrews 13:17.

debates.bearing: The three need not compete. The first hearers would have thought of those whom God had appointed to speak and pray for Zion, while the pattern extends to everyone who calls on the LORD. What matters is the purpose: to keep God's promises before Him until they are fulfilled.

debates.question: Does the coming Savior of verse 11 refer to the first or the second coming of Christ?

views.label: The first coming
views.case: Matthew 21:5 draws on the opening words of the verse, 'Say to the Daughter of Zion', when Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey. The Hebrew can be read 'your salvation comes', and Jesus' name means 'the LORD saves', Matthew 1:21. On this reading the verse announces the arrival of salvation in the person of Jesus.

views.label: The second coming
views.case: The verse speaks of reward and recompense going with Him, which Revelation 22:12 repeats: 'Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done.' The names of verse 12 and the full restoration of Zion also point to a coming that is still ahead.

views.label: Both, in a single movement of promise
views.case: The prophets often look at the coming of God as one scene in which near and far events are seen together. The first coming fulfils the announcement and opens salvation, and the second brings the reward and the full establishing of the city. This reading follows the pattern of Jesus' use of Isaiah 61.

debates.bearing: The third view fits the New Testament's habit of treating Isaiah's promises as being fulfilled in stages. The Savior has come, as Matthew shows, and will come again, as Revelation says, and the verse can bear both.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with two verbs of silence, echesheh and eshqot, 'I will not keep silent' and 'I will not keep still'. The first, from chashah, is picked up in verse 6 when the watchmen 'will never be silent', with the same verb. The LORD's refusal to be silent and the watchmen's refusal to be silent are one commitment seen from two sides. Verse 7 then turns to the word domi, translated 'rest', which means quiet or stillness. The watchmen are told to give Him no quiet, as the BSB's 'rest' conveys.

The phrase 'you who call on the LORD' in verse 6 translates a Hebrew participle that is literally 'you who remind the LORD', from the root zakar, to remember, in a causative form. The people who stand on the wall are those who cause the LORD to remember, that is, who bring His promises before Him. It is a bold image for prayer, and it explains why the watchmen's speech is so persistent. The verb for 'posted' in verse 6 is from the root paqad, to appoint or assign, and it indicates that these are not volunteers but those given a duty by the LORD.

In verse 4 the new names are hephtzi-bah, which the footnote gives as 'My delight is in her', and be'ulah, 'married'. The word behind Beulah is related to the verb ba'al, to marry or to be master, and verse 5 uses the same verb: 'as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you.' So the name and the verb that follows it rhyme. The old names, Azubah and Shemamah, come from the root for being left behind and for desolation, and Azubah is the name of Jehoshaphat's mother, 1 Kings 22:42, as Hephzibah is of Manasseh's mother, 2 Kings 21:1. The prophet picks everyday names and gives them a new sense, and at the end of the chapter he does it again. 'A City Not Forsaken' in verse 12 uses the verb for forsaking in the passive, from the same root as Azubah, so that the city that was named Forsaken is now named Not Forsaken.

'Sought Out' in verse 12 is derushah, from darash, to seek or inquire. The city once left alone with no one passing through, Isaiah 60:15, is now a place people seek. The names 'Holy People' and 'Redeemed of the LORD' recall Sinai, where Israel was to be a holy nation, Exodus 19:6. The word for redeemed is the one connected to the goel, the Redeemer of Isaiah 59:20 and 60:16, so the people are those whom the Redeemer has bought back.

In verse 11 the LORD's proclamation to the ends of the earth says, 'See, your Savior comes.' The Hebrew word translated Savior is a noun from the root yasha, to save, and it is the same root that gives the name of Jesus, Yeshua, as in Matthew 1:21. The phrase can be read as 'your salvation comes', and both senses fit, since in the Hebrew mind salvation and the one who brings it come together. The next lines, 'His reward is with Him, and His recompense goes before Him', repeat the words of Isaiah 40:10 exactly, so that the voice that opened the second half of the book in chapter 40 is heard again as the book nears its close.

Finally, in verse 3 the city is 'a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD'. The positions are striking: usually a crown is worn on the head and not held in the hand. The text pictures God holding His people as something precious, on display and kept safe at once. It sits well with the promise that He has inscribed Zion on the palms of His hands, Isaiah 49:16.

typology.type: The bridegroom who rejoices over his bride, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The marriage between God and His people is a recurring picture in the prophets, Hosea 2:19-20 and Isaiah 54:5. Jesus takes the role of the bridegroom when asked why His disciples do not fast, Matthew 9:15, and John the Baptist says that the bride belongs to the bridegroom, John 3:29. Paul describes Christ giving Himself up for the church to present her to Himself in splendour, Ephesians 5:25-27, and Revelation 19:7-8 and 21:2 depict the wedding of the Lamb and the city prepared as a bride. The type is imperfect: the prophet's picture speaks of God rejoicing over a city, while the New Testament shows the Bridegroom paying the price of the bride's redemption with His own life.

typology.type: The new name from the LORD's mouth, verses 2 and 4
typology.fulfillment: A name given by God marks a new identity, as with Abraham and Israel, Genesis 17:5 and 32:28. For Zion the new name replaces shame with delight. In Christ, the same pattern becomes personal. Simon is renamed, John 1:42, and believers are told that they will receive a new name, Revelation 2:17, and the name of God and of the new Jerusalem, Revelation 3:12. Peter says that those who were not a people are now the people of God, 1 Peter 2:10, which echoes Hosea 2:23. The type falls short in that an earthly renaming could be undone by later failure, whereas the names given in Christ are held by His faithfulness.

typology.type: The watchmen who never keep silent, verses 6 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The persistent watch of the posted watchmen is a pattern for persistent prayer. Jesus teaches that God will bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night, Luke 18:7, and Paul urges believers to pray without ceasing, 1 Thessalonians 5:17. At a higher level, Christ Himself 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25, so the persistent advocacy on Zion's behalf is carried by the Son at the right hand of the Father, Romans 8:34. The watchmen of the Old Testament had to be replaced and could fall asleep, Isaiah 56:10. Christ does not.

typology.type: The herald and the highway, verses 10 to 11
typology.fulfillment: The people are told to prepare the way and clear away stones, and the herald announces the Savior's coming. The Gospels take up this language when John the Baptist is identified as the voice calling to prepare the way for the Lord, Matthew 3:3, quoting Isaiah 40:3. At the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:5 uses the opening words of verse 11, the crowds spread cloaks on the road, and the King comes as the Daughter of Zion's salvation. The correspondence is real, but the entry is a small version of the final coming, for the reward that goes with Him will be given when He returns, Revelation 22:12.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most clearly through the figure of the bridegroom and the announcement of verse 11. Matthew's account of the entry into Jerusalem begins with the words 'Say to the Daughter of Zion', which are those of Isaiah 62:11, and continues with Zechariah 9:9, 'See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey', Matthew 21:5. Matthew is saying that the herald's message to Zion has found its moment. The crowds spread their cloaks on the road, as if the highway of verse 10 were being prepared, and they cry 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord', Matthew 21:8-9. The name of the child, Jesus, means that the LORD saves, and the phrase 'your salvation comes' in verse 11 is a statement a Christian reader hears with that name in mind.

The chapter also leads to Christ as the Bridegroom. The Old Testament speaks of God as the husband of His people, Isaiah 54:5. In the Gospels Jesus claims the place without hesitation, saying that the guests of the bridegroom cannot mourn while He is with them, Matthew 9:15. John the Baptist calls Him the bridegroom and rejoices to hear His voice, John 3:29. Paul explains what the bridegroom has done: Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to sanctify her and present her to Himself, 'glorious, without stain or wrinkle', Ephesians 5:25-27. Isaiah promised that God would rejoice over His bride, and the New Testament shows the price at which the bride was won.

The names of verse 12 are given to a people in Christ. 'The Redeemed of the LORD' becomes the church redeemed by His blood, as Titus 2:14 says, 'He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession.' The 'Holy People' is the language Peter uses of the church, 1 Peter 2:9. The city that was Forsaken is 'Sought Out', and Jesus says of Himself that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10. The one who knocks on the door of the city is the one who seeks.

The chapter also tells of a reward that goes with Him. In Isaiah, the reward and recompense accompany the Savior, and Revelation 22:12 has Jesus say, 'Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me.' The word of Isaiah is thus given to Christ in the last chapter of the Bible. And the final scene, the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2, is the chapter's goal.

Care is needed in how far to press the details. The chapter is addressed to Zion and to Israel's watchmen, and its first meaning is about the restoration of a particular people. The links to Christ rest on the New Testament's own use of the language, in Matthew 21:5, Revelation 22:12 and the marriage passages, and not on finding a hidden meaning in the oath about grain or the stones of the highway. What Isaiah supplies is the promise, and Christ supplies the Bridegroom.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as one who speaks and does not rest. 'For Zion's sake I will not keep silent.' The silence of God is a theme in Isaiah's later chapters, where the people wonder whether He is holding back, Isaiah 64:12. The reply here is that He will not be silent about their shame, and He will not let His own purpose go unspoken. His speech is effective: when He speaks a name, it takes hold.

He is a God who delights. The central verses speak of Him taking delight and rejoicing over His people as a bridegroom does over his bride. It is easy to think of God's love as a kind of duty, and the prophets will not allow it. Zephaniah says He will rejoice over His people with singing, Zephaniah 3:17. The doctrine of God's joy fits with His self-sufficiency: He does not need His people, yet He is glad in them, and the gladness is a free overflow of love.

God keeps His oath. In verse 8 He swears by His right hand and mighty arm that the enemies will not eat the grain again. The Bible says elsewhere that when God wanted to give assurance He swore by Himself, since there was no one greater, Hebrews 6:13. The oath is a way of bending Himself toward human weakness, giving the people something to hold on to when circumstances say otherwise.

He is a God who works through His people. He appoints the watchmen, He sends the herald, and He tells the people to clear the highway. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility are not opposed here. He has already said He will act, and yet He tells them to pray without rest and to prepare. The doctrine is that God's purposes are certain and that His people have a real part in how they come about.

He is holy and a redeemer. The people are called holy and redeemed, and the Holy One of Israel is the one who redeems. His reward is with Him, and His recompense goes before Him, a reminder that He is also a judge who rewards and repays. The marriage and the oath, the delight and the reward, are not contradictions. They describe the same God from different sides.

For worship, the chapter calls us to pray with the persistence of watchmen, trusting that the promises we bring are His own. It invites us to receive our names from Him rather than from our past. And it asks us to answer His rejoicing over us with our own, in the words of the verse before this one, 'I will rejoice greatly in the LORD', Isaiah 61:10.

crossReferences.note: Zion says the LORD has forsaken her, and He answers that a mother may forget her child but He will not forget Zion, who is inscribed on His palms. Isaiah 62 answers the same complaint with a new name, 'a city not forsaken', and shows that the earlier promise is being kept.

The forsaken wife is told her Maker is her husband, the Holy One of Israel her Redeemer, and that the LORD has called her back. It is the marriage picture in its first form in this part of Isaiah, and Isaiah 62:4-5 carries it forward to the point of rejoicing and renaming.

Israel's watchmen are blind, oblivious and mute dogs that cannot bark. Placed beside Isaiah 62:6, where the watchmen never fall silent, the verses show a reversal in leadership. God does not leave His city to the old guards, but appoints watchmen who will speak and pray until He acts.

The herald is told to say 'Here is your God' and the reward and recompense are with Him. Isaiah 62:11 repeats the same lines word for word, so the book that began with comfort ends its main movement with the same announcement, now closer to its arrival.

The covenant curse was that a people the Israelites did not know would eat the produce of their land and all their toil. The oath of Isaiah 62:8 reverses that curse directly, and shows that the promise is the undoing of covenant judgment rather than a general wish for prosperity.

The LORD says He will betroth His people to Himself forever, in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and compassion. The language of betrothal prepares for Isaiah 62:5. The pairing shows that the marriage image was a settled prophetic way of describing the covenant between God and Israel.

The LORD is among His people, mighty to save, rejoicing over them with gladness and singing. It gives voice to what Isaiah 62:5 states: that God's rejoicing is personal and audible. The two passages together make a strong claim about the joy that God takes in those He saves.

Matthew begins the quotation with 'Say to the Daughter of Zion', the opening of Isaiah 62:11, and adds Zechariah 9:9 at the entry into Jerusalem. The messenger's announcement is connected to the arrival of the King, so that Jesus' entry is seen as the moment the herald's word finds its answer.

Jesus tells the parable of the widow to show that people should pray at all times, and asks whether God will not bring justice for His elect who cry to Him day and night. The language matches the watchmen of Isaiah 62:6-7, who never fall silent, and gives the persistence of prayer a New Testament home.

The one who overcomes will receive the name of God, the name of the new Jerusalem and Christ's new name. The renaming promised to Zion is extended to each believer, who is marked as belonging to God and to His city. The link shows that Isaiah's names are still being given.

John sees the holy city arrive as a bride dressed for her husband, and hears that God's dwelling is with humanity. Isaiah 62:5 reaches its goal in this scene, where the Bridegroom lives among those He has won. It closes the story of the city that was once left alone and without a name.

Christ says, 'Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me.' The words repeat the language of Isaiah 62:11 and 40:10 and place them on the lips of Jesus. The promise that the reward goes with the Savior is thus fulfilled by His own announcement at the close of the Bible.

study.oneStory:
Scripture's story begins with a marriage, a man and a woman joined in a garden and unashamed, Genesis 2:24-25. The fall brings shame and separation, and from that point the Bible is the account of how God sets about winning back a people for Himself. It is told in many images, rescue, adoption, redemption and temple, but the marriage image is one of the deepest. The prophets say that Israel is the wife of the LORD, that she has been unfaithful, and that He will take her back. Isaiah 62 is where that long story finds its most tender expression: the one who was Forsaken and Desolate is renamed Delight and Married.

The chapter also answers the question of how a people who lost everything can have hope. The exile had stripped Israel of land, temple and kingship. The returned community was small and often discouraged. Isaiah's answer is that their identity does not depend on their present condition. It depends on a name that God gives and an oath that God swears. This is the logic of the whole covenant: God's promise creates what it declares.

Within the book of Isaiah, the chapter closes the movement that began in chapter 60. The light has come, the herald has spoken, and now the city has a name and is awaiting its Savior. Chapter 63 brings the warrior in stained garments, and chapters 65 and 66 show the new heavens and the new earth, in which God rejoices in Jerusalem and delights in His people, Isaiah 65:17-19. The marriage of 62 is therefore set between rescue and new creation.

The New Testament tells how the Bridegroom came. Jesus comes to Zion on a donkey, gives Himself for the church and rises, and He sends out watchmen of a new kind, His people who pray and herald the news to the ends of the earth. The names of Isaiah 62 are given to those in Christ, who are called a holy people, a people for His own possession, 1 Peter 2:9, and who will bear His name.

The end is a wedding. John sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven prepared as a bride adorned for her husband, and hears that God will dwell with His people and wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:2-4. The cry 'Come' of the Spirit and the bride, Revelation 22:17, answers the watchmen's long prayer. Those once called Forsaken are called Sought Out, and the God who would not keep silent speaks the final word of the Bible, 'Behold, I am coming soon.'

quiz.q: What do the new names Hephzibah and Beulah replace, and what do they mean?

options.text: They replace Forsaken and Desolate, meaning My Delight Is in Her and Married.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly gives this contrast and meaning.

options.text: They replace Blessed and Holy with names of judgment.
options.note: The movement is from shame to delight, not from blessing to judgment.

options.text: They are simply geographic place names with no symbolic meaning.
options.note: The names are explicitly symbolic, reversing the meaning of Forsaken and Desolate.

options.text: They describe only a change in the city's physical architecture.
options.note: Rebuilding does appear elsewhere in this section, but these specific names describe relational and covenantal status, not architecture.

quiz.q: What are the watchmen in verses 6-7 commanded to do?

options.text: Never be silent, taking no rest themselves and giving God no rest until Jerusalem is established as the praise of the earth.
options.note: Verses 6-7 give this explicit, persistent commission.

options.text: Guard the city only against physical military attack.
options.note: Watchmen do guard walls elsewhere in Scripture, but here their role is persistent calling on the LORD in prayer, not solely physical defense.

options.text: Remain silent so as not to disturb God's rest.
options.note: The opposite; they are told never to be silent and to give God no rest.

options.text: Take turns resting in shifts with no urgency implied.
options.note: The text emphasizes urgency, they will never be silent day or night.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply the bridegroom-and-bride imagery of verse 5?

options.text: Paul applies it to Christ's love for the church, sanctifying her as His bride, Ephesians 5:25-27.
options.note: Ephesians 5 draws directly on this marital covenant imagery.

options.text: It is applied only to human marriages with no theological significance.
options.note: Human marriage does reflect this pattern, but its primary New Testament application is theological, Christ's love for the church.

options.text: The New Testament never uses bridal imagery for God's people.
options.note: Ephesians 5 and Revelation 19, 21 use this imagery extensively.

options.text: It is used to describe the relationship between Israel and pagan nations.
options.note: The bridal imagery describes covenant intimacy between God, or Christ, and His own people, not pagan nations.

quiz.q: What does the herald announce in verse 11, and how does it connect to the Gospels?

options.text: Behold, your Savior comes, echoed in Matthew's description of Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
options.note: Matthew 21:5 draws on this kind of herald language for Jesus' entry.

options.text: It announces a military victory with no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: It is directly connected to Christ's coming in the Gospels.

options.text: It predicts the rebuilding of the temple only, unrelated to any messianic figure.
options.note: Rebuilding is a theme elsewhere in this section, but this specific announcement centers on a coming Savior, directly applied to Christ.

options.text: It is addressed only to foreign kings, not to Zion herself.
options.note: It is explicitly addressed to Daughter Zion, telling her that her Savior comes.

questions: Zion was renamed from Forsaken to My Delight Is in Her. What old, shame-based name or identity are you still carrying that God wants to replace with His delight over you?
The watchmen were commanded to give God no rest until His promises were fulfilled. Is there a promise of God you have stopped actively, persistently praying for?
God is pictured as a bridegroom rejoicing over Zion as his bride. Does your relationship with God feel like duty or performance, or does it carry the warmth of being delighted in?
The people were told to prepare the way, clear the stones, and raise a banner for the nations. What practical step could you take this week to prepare the way for someone else to meet God?
Zion's final new name is Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken. Where do you need to remember that God actively seeks you out rather than waiting for you to find your own way back?

translationNotes.note: Hephzibah and Beulah are transliterated Hebrew names rather than translated in most English versions; the BSB gives both the transliteration and the meaning to preserve the wordplay of renaming.
Sought Out translates a rare term implying deliberate, active pursuit, reinforcing that Zion's restoration comes from God's initiative rather than her own effort to be found.
